title: Gradient Boosting
learning_outcomes: Explain gradient boosting and accurately refer to at least two syllabus subtopics.
Apply the main idea of gradient boosting to a small example, trace, calculation, or scenario.
Identify one important assumption or failure mode and describe how to check it.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study gradient boosting in the context of supervised machine learning. You will connect the PDF subtopics to a small example and practice describing what the evidence does—and does not—support.
content.why_it_matters: Gradient Boosting matters because it affects how data is collected, represented, analyzed, interpreted, or used in a decision. Check the task and assumptions before choosing a method.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: Supervised learning fits a mapping from labeled examples to predictions. Algorithm choice should follow data structure, decision costs, interpretability needs, and fair evaluation.

items.title: Boosting fundamentals
items.text: Define boosting fundamentals in relation to gradient boosting; identify the input, output, assumptions, and who uses the result.

items.title: Sequential error correction
items.text: Work through sequential error correction using a small, synthetic example before scaling up. State what the calculation or method returns and why that result is useful.

items.title: Gradient boosting for regression
items.text: Check the edge cases for gradient boosting for regression: missing values, unusual ranges, different groups, time boundaries, or a changed input can affect the conclusion.

content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the provided synthetic input, rerun or retrace the example, and change one value at a time. Do not use personal records, credentials, or data you are not authorized to access.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: Keep the question, data grain, units, and assumptions explicit. If a result differs, inspect the input and steps in order. Avoid turning an observed association into a causal claim, treating a sample as the population, or assuming a small demonstration guarantees production behavior. Classification probabilities become decisions only after a threshold and consequences are considered.

content_blocks.title: Responsible interpretation
content_blocks.text: This example is a teaching aid. It is static in the CodeLeaf lesson and is not executed in the browser. It uses small synthetic values; validate any real workflow in a separate, appropriate local environment and protect sensitive data.

content_blocks.text: Recap: Supervised learning fits a mapping from labeled examples to predictions. content.task: Try it yourself: create a small synthetic example for gradient boosting. State a question, make a prediction, trace or run an appropriate calculation, then write one finding and one limitation.
task_acceptance_criteria: Refer accurately to the topic and its syllabus subtopics.
Record a reproducible example or a complete manual trace with an expected result.
Document at least one assumption, limitation, data-quality issue, or evaluation check.
hints: Write down the input, expected result, units, and assumptions first.
Change only one condition when testing a revised example.
Ask whether the data and method represent the real decision; do not infer causality or production readiness from a toy example.
troubleshooting: Check input values, path assumptions, package versions, indentation, and units.
For SQL, use a local schema and read-only test data; this page does not provide a live database.
For package-dependent work, create an isolated environment and use the relevant official documentation.
